paper_title: Evaluating Memanto on DolphinBench for AI Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Memory benchmarks built on question answering tell an agent which fact to recall. Workplace requests often leave that need implicit: to post an update in the team's channel, an agent must work out which channel from earlier interactions and use it in a tool call. We evaluate Memanto, a memory agent that ranks memories with an information-theoretic relevance score, on DolphinBench, which tests memory through 600 simulated workplace tasks, each validated as requiring memory. Running in the Hermes agent harness with GPT-6-Luna and at most 6 iterations per conversation, Memanto completes 503 tasks (83.83%). The strongest configuration reported by the benchmark's authors, Mem0 with GPT-5.6-Luna and up to 60 iterations, completes 424 (70.67%). Memanto's run also has the lowest total cost ($10.86, against $61.48 for the cheapest reported run) and the shortest median task latency (15.32s). Grading uses the benchmark's own judge, but the agent model differs, so these results compare complete systems. The memory system affects both whether an agent completes such tasks and what completion costs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: AI agents increasingly carry out long-running work such as software engineering, web tasks, and customer service. This work depends on information from earlier sessions and project histories that no longer fits in the agents context window. Memory systems retain this information and return it when the agent needs it (Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025; Rasmussen et al., 2025), and memory benchmarks measure how well they do so. Most memory benchmarks pose questions about long conversation history (Maharana et al., 2024). Later benchmarks added temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention (Wu et al., 2025), and histories beyond million tokens (Tavakoli et al., 2025), but kept the question-answering format. question names what to retrieve: Which messaging platform does the team use? tells the system what to recall. An instruction such as Post an update in the teams channel does not. The agent must recognize that the request depends 1 on an earlier interaction, retrieve the right detail, and use it correctly in tool call. Evaluating memory for agents therefore calls for tasks in which the needed information must be identified, retrieved, and acted on. Benchmark quality matters as much as format. An audit of LoCoMo found incorrect answers in 6.4% of its non-adversarial questions (99 of 1,540) (Penfield Labs, 2026), and community reports identified arithmetic errors and mislabeled evidence in LongMemEval (LongMemEval contributors, 2025). BEAM uses human review to check that its questions are answerable (Tavakoli et al., 2025), but an answerable task need not require memory: capable model may solve it from the request alone. DolphinBench (Rathi et al., 2026) addresses both concerns. Its 600 tasks are workplace actions carried out through simulated applications, and each task is kept only if an agent passes it in two runs when given the relevant history and fails it in two runs without that history. Every task is therefore solvable and depends on memory. The benchmark also requires every result to report accuracy together with total cost and median task latency, so accuracy cannot be bought with unreported spending or waiting time. We evaluate Memanto (Abtahi et al., 2026b) on DolphinBench (Figure 2). Memanto is memory agent that selects memories with information-theoretic scoring (Abtahi et al., 2026a). In the Hermes agent harness (Nous Research, 2026) with GPT-6-Luna, Memanto completes 503 of 600 tasks (83.83%), at total cost of $10.86 and median task latency of 15.32 (Figure 1). The strongest result reported by the benchmarks authors, Mem0 in the same harness with GPT-5.6-Luna, completes 424 tasks (70.67%) at $96.21 and 37.69 s. Our contributions are: complete DolphinBench run of Memanto, reporting accuracy, cost split between the agent model and memory, and median latency, as the benchmark requires, with the scripts and results of the run released for reproduction1; 1github.com/moorcheh-ai/memanto-benchmark per-persona comparison with the official runs, showing that Memantos accuracy is stable across the three personas (83.0 85.0%), including the persona every reported run found hardest; an of analysis how threshold-based information-theoretic retrieval may help when facts are revised across sessions, and of what comparison with runs that differ in agent model and agent settings can and cannot show.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Memory benchmarks. LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) evaluate memory through questions about long multi-session conversations; LongMemEval covers information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. BEAM (Tavakoli et al., 2025) extends conversations beyond million tokens. MemBench (Tan et al., 2025) and MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026) evaluate memory in LLM agents, the latter by delivering information incrementally over many turns. newer line of work evaluates memory through agent tasks: MEMTRACK (Deshpande et al., 2025) evaluates memory and state tracking across multiplatform workplace environments, MemoryArena (He et al., 2026) links sessions so that later subtasks depend on earlier ones, and Mem2ActBench (Shen et al., 2026) tests whether agents use long-term memory in taskoriented actions. DolphinBench (Rathi et al., 2026) belongs to this line and adds per-task validation against memory and mandatory reporting of cost and latency. Memory systems for agents. MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) manages tiers of context in the manner of an operating system. Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) extracts and consolidates salient facts from conversations, Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025) organizes memory as temporal knowledge graph, and Hindsight (Latimer et al., 2025) structures memory around retaining, recalling, and reflect2 1 Ingestion once per persona 2 Task execution once per task: 600 tasks, 200 per persona Persona history 3,4005,128 dated user messages (500k tokens) Task request new conversation for every task Hermes agent GPT-6-Luna 6 iterations per task tool calls results Simulated applications Notion, Gmail, GitHub, calendar, CRM, deployment Hermes agent saves one new conversation per message; Memanto remember tool Frozen memory writes confirmed, then snapshotted; read only in tests recall call ranked memories final state and trace read only Memanto recall ITS score 0.1 top =50 memories Grading deterministic checks + LLM judge (GPT-5.6-Sol) pass only if every check passes Figure 2: How Memanto was evaluated on DolphinBench. During ingestion, the Hermes agent reads each dated history message in new conversation and saves what it should remember through Memantos remember tool; every write is confirmed searchable, and the memory is then frozen. For each of the 600 tasks (200 per persona), the agent starts new conversation, calls Memantos recall tool, which returns memories ranked by information-theoretic scoring (ITS), and completes the task through simulated applications. task passes only when every deterministic and LLM-judged check passes. ing. Honcho (Plastic Labs, 2025) and Supermemory (Supermemory, 2025) are opensource memory systems for agents, and agent harnesses such as Hermes (Nous Research, 2026) include built-in memory. Memanto (Abtahi et al., 2026b) represents memories as typed semantic records and retrieves them with information-theoretic scoring (Abtahi et al., 2026a); Section 4 describes the configuration we evaluate.

sections.title: 3 DolphinBench
sections.content: DolphinBench (Rathi et al., 2026) evaluates memory through task completion rather than question answering. It covers three knowledgework personas: Morgan, startup CEO; Alex, an infrastructure engineer; and Riley, product manager. Each persona has simulated history spanning several years, with 3,4005,128 user messages (about 500k tokens). The histories embed changing details in everyday conversation, so an agent must notice what is relevant, track updates, and tell current information from outdated information. After processing personas history, the agent completes 200 tasks for that persona, 600 in total. Tasks are workplace actions carried out through simulated applications, such as Notion, Gmail, and GitHub, and calendar, email, CRM, and deployment tools. The task request and the application records give the immediate context, but they do not say which earlier interaction holds the needed detail: the agent must recognize that memory is needed and decide what to retrieve. To validate task, the benchmark authors ran GPT-5.6-Luna twice with the relevant (oracle) messages and twice without them; task was kept only if both runs with the messages passed every check and both runs without them failed.

sections.title: 4 Memanto
sections.content: Memanto (Abtahi et al., 2026b) is memory It gives agent for long-horizon AI agents. an agent two tools: remember, which saves memory, and recall, which returns the memories most relevant to query. The agent decides when to call them. Relevance is computed with information-theoretic scoring (ITS) from Moorcheh (Abtahi et al., 2026a), which scores binarized representations exhaustively rather than through an approximate nearestneighbour index, so the same query over the same memories always returns the same rank3 ing. Two settings control what reaches the agent. score threshold decides which memories qualify, and retrieval limit caps how many enter the agents context. We use threshold of 0.1 and limit of = 50. On the ITS scale, scores below 0.1 form the lowest relevance band, labeled irrelevant (Moorcheh AI, 2026), so this threshold removes only memories that ITS rates as irrelevant, while the limit bounds the size, and therefore the cost, of the agents context.

sections.title: 5 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Systems compared. We ran Memanto in the Hermes agent harness (Nous Research, 2026) with GPT-6-Luna as the agent model. We compare it with the five memory configurations that Rathi et al. (2026) evaluated in the same harness: Hermes built-in memory, Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), Honcho (Plastic Labs, 2025), Hindsight (Latimer et al., 2025), and Supermemory (Supermemory, 2025). Their figures are taken from Table 2 of Rathi et al. (2026), where all five use GPT-5.6-Luna; we did not re-run them. Per-persona scores and the split of agent cost between ingestion and tests come from the official run records released with the benchmark (Mem0, 2026). Figure 1 also shows the official runs with MiniMax M3 in Hermes and with Claude Sonnet 5 in Claude Code. Agent settings. Our run uses medium reasoning effort and in each stage, only the tools that stage needs: Memantos remember during ingestion, and the tasks simulated application with Memantos recall during tests. Protocol. Our run has the two stages DolphinBench defines: the full history of persona is processed before any test is taken. Ingestion: as the official protocol requires, the Hermes agent processes each personas history messages in order, one new conversation per message. Its only tool is Memantos remember, and an ingestion instruction asks it to save the information in the message, preserving dates, amounts, names, and corrections. Automatic capture is disabled, so the memory holds only what the agent chooses to save, and each write is confirmed to be searchable before the run continues. The completed memory is then frozen: its contents are snapshotted and hashed, and before testing the live memory is checked against the snapshot. Task execution: for each task, the agent starts new conversation with the tasks application tools and Memantos recall tool (ITS threshold 0.1, = 50), and completes the task through the simulated applications. Memory writes are blocked during tests. Freezing memory and starting every task in new conversation keeps tasks independent: nothing learned while solving one task can help with another. The official protocol requires both: fresh conversation for each test, and memory that tests cannot change (Mem0, 2026). The scripts for both stages and the results of our run are in the accompanying repository.1 Metrics. We report the three measures DolphinBench requires. Accuracy is the percentage of the 600 tasks passed. Grading combines deterministic checks, for requirements such as tool calls, identifiers, dates, and values, with an LLM judge for requirements that need semantic interpretation (Zheng et al., 2023); task passes only when every check passes. As in the reported runs, the judge is GPT-5.6-Sol, the benchmarks own, with its grading prompts and verdict logic unchanged. Cost is the total spent on ingestion and on the 600 tasks, split into agent-model tokens, as estimated by Hermes from the recorded API usage, and memory operations, measured as the Moorcheh Cloud usage credits the run consumed. Latency is the median time per task, including tool use.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: Why retrieval may matter for action. One possible explanation for these results is how Memanto selects records for the agent. Action tasks often depend on facts that change: request may depend on preference stated in one interaction and revised several sessions later. If retrieval returns only the earlier passage, the agent can identify the right preference and still act on an outdated value. threshold that admits every memory not rated irrelevant, combined with generous limit, makes it more likely that both the original statement and its revision reach the agent, which can then resolve the update before acting. We have not isolated this effect; an ablation over the threshold and the limit, and an analysis of the 97 failed tasks, would test it. Where the cost and latency differences come from. In the reported Hermes runs, most of the agent cost was spent during ingestion, when the agent processed the persona histories. 6 The official run records put agent inference for the 600 tests themselves at $3.23 (Mem0) to $8.05 (built-in memory), out of $57.99$96.56 in agent cost overall (Mem0, 2026). In our run the agent also processed every history message, yet its agent cost for ingestion and tests together was $2.17. Several factors contribute: the agent had single tool and short prompt during ingestion; it used medium rather than high reasoning effort and at most 6 rather than 60 iterations per conversation; bounded retrieval (at most 50 memories) kept its context small during tests; and GPT-6-Luna and GPT5.6-Luna may differ in price and speed. The same factors bear on latency. The iteration limit and reasoning effort constrain the agent, so they are more likely to lower accuracy than to raise it, yet the run completed more tasks than any reported run. Whether the reported systems would keep their accuracy under the same limits is untested; our data do not separate the effect of memory from that of the model and settings, and run of the baselines with our settings, or of Memanto with theirs, would. Memory-side cost depends less on the agent. Memantos $8.69 is the Moorcheh Cloud usage credits the run consumed, against $26.66 $281.79 for the four external memory systems in the reported runs. self-hosted Moorcheh deployment would remove this usage charge, leaving only the cost of running its infrastructure.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We evaluated Memanto on DolphinBench, where an agent must act on information from earlier interactions without being told what to retrieve. In the Hermes harness with GPT-6-Luna, Memanto completed 503 of 600 tasks (83.83%) at total cost of $10.86 and median task latency of 15.32 s, each better than every configuration reported by the benchmarks authors. It did so with at most 6 agent iterations per conversation, tenth of those allowed in the reported runs. Because the runs also differ in agent model, the comparison is between complete systems; controlled runs with matched models and settings, ablations of the retrieval settings, and repeated trials are the natural next steps. We release the scripts and results of this study at github.com/moorcheh-ai/ memanto-benchmark so that others can repeat the run and carry out these comparisons; at $10.86 for full run, doing so is inexpensive. Benchmarks such as DolphinBench, which validate every task against memory and require cost and latency alongside accuracy, make such comparisons possible. They show that the choice of memory system decides not only what an agent can recall, but whether it completes the work, and at what cost.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Different agent model and settings. The reported baselines used GPT-5.6-Luna with high reasoning effort and up to 60 iterations per conversation; our run used GPT-6-Luna with medium reasoning effort. different model may complete more tasks, use fewer tokens, or respond faster regardless of the memory system, and tighter limits lower cost and latency, so the gaps in Table 1 cannot be attributed to Memanto alone. Cost accounting. Our agent cost is Hermess own estimate from recorded API usage, with retries not audited separately, and our memory cost is Moorcheh Cloud usage credits. The reported costs follow the benchmarks own accounting, so the two may differ in what they include. Reported, not re-run, baselines. Baseline figures come from Rathi et al. (2026). Harness versions, provider prices, and infrastructure may differ between their runs and ours.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Several authors are affiliated with EdgeAI Innovations Inc., which develops Memanto and the Moorcheh retrieval engine it uses. To reduce the risk of bias, we use public benchmark with fixed tasks, the benchmarks own grading checks, prompts, and judge, and baseline figures reported by the benchmarks authors rather than our own runs of competing systems, and we state the differences in agent model and settings throughout. So that our results can be checked independently, we release the scripts and results of this study in the accompanying repository.1 DolphinBench personas are synthetic, and no personal data was used.
